questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish its question from the broader build-vs-buy decision covered in Lesson 4?
options: It is a sharper, more technical follow-up: once you've already decided to buy, what specifically do you give up technically by choosing a managed package rather than writing equivalent custom Apex
It is exactly the same question, just repeated for emphasis
It only applies to orgs with fewer than 100 users
It replaces the need to ever consider cost or functional fit
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates the broader decision of whether to buy (Lesson 4) from this narrower, technical question of what a managed package specifically locks away once you've decided to buy.

questions.q: What does 'namespacing' do to a managed package's components, per this lesson?
options: It deletes the components after one year
It assigns a unique prefix to every field, object, and class the package creates, preventing naming collisions and marking the component as vendor-owned and not directly editable
It automatically converts the package's Apex into Flow elements
It grants subscribers full edit access to the package's Apex source
questions.explain: Namespacing both prevents naming collisions with the rest of the org and marks a component as something the subscriber doesn't own and can't directly edit -- the specific technical cost this lesson focuses on.

questions.q: Which of the following does this lesson identify as a genuine, deliberately exposed extension point a managed package might offer?
options: Directly editing the package's hidden Apex classes
Renaming the package's namespace to match the subscriber org's own naming convention
An invocable Apex method a Flow can call, or a platform event the package fires that subscriber code can subscribe to
Disabling the package's AppExchange security review after installation
questions.explain: Well-built packages often ship specific hooks like invocable methods or platform events precisely so subscribers can extend behavior without needing access to the hidden source.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what distinguishes a genuine configuration extension point from something that only 'looks exposed'?
options: There is no real distinction -- any setting visible in the UI counts as a genuine extension point
Genuine extension points require a separate AppExchange purchase to unlock
Genuine extension points are always implemented as Apex triggers

A genuine extension point (a real custom setting or custom metadata type) gives the org actual control, while something that only looks adjustable may just toggle between a small number of vendor-chosen behaviors rather than real configurability
questions.explain: The lesson specifically calls out the importance of distinguishing real configuration surface from a setting that merely appears adjustable but doesn't give the org meaningful control -- this distinction matters during evaluation, before committing to the package.

questions.q: What criterion does this lesson give for judging how risky a managed package's constraints are for a given org?
options: How often the org's own process actually changes, since a stable process is a safer long-term bet under a package's constraints than a process the org revises frequently
Whether the package's logo is professionally designed
Whether the package was the first result in an AppExchange search
Whether the vendor is headquartered in the same country as the subscriber
questions.explain: A package covering a stable process collides with unsupported requirements less often than one covering a process that changes every quarter -- frequent change means frequent collisions with whatever the package doesn't let you configure.
